analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the 20% tax deduction for income from pass-through businesses.
analysis.headline: 194 members cosponsored the bill, but the House Ways and Means Committee never scheduled action on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law gives owners of pass-through businesses — partnerships, S-corps, and sole proprietorships — a deduction worth 20% of their qualified business income. That deduction is scheduled to expire after 2025. This bill deletes the expiration date, making the deduction permanent. It drew 194 cosponsors, almost all Republicans, but was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of pass-through businesses — partnerships, S-corps, and sole proprietorships — who would keep the 20% deduction beyond its scheduled 2025 expiration. Because a percentage deduction is worth more in dollars the higher the income, the largest gains would go to owners with the biggest business incomes, not to the smallest firms.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes the subsection of tax code Section 199A that schedules the qualified business income deduction to expire after December 31, 2025, making the 20% deduction permanent.

Qualified business income is the net income from a trade or business, excluding capital gains, dividends, interest income, and income earned outside the U.S., so the deduction reaches owners of operating businesses across the economy.
Making the deduction permanent would give business owners certainty that the tax break continues in every future year, rather than lapsing at the end of 2025 under current law.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, which forgoes the revenue from the deduction every year permanently instead of letting it expire in 2025. Over time that means more federal borrowing, or higher taxes and reduced services elsewhere, borne by taxpayers at large.

drawbacks.text: Making the deduction permanent means the federal government gives up that revenue every year going forward, rather than letting it lapse after 2025 as scheduled, adding to deficits or requiring offsetting cuts or tax increases.

The deduction is worth 20% of a business's qualified income, so its dollar value rises with income; the largest benefits would flow to owners of the most profitable pass-through enterprises, a group that skews toward high earners, even though ordinary small business owners also claim it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real certainty to small business owners who currently plan around the deduction's 2025 expiration. But the cost-benefit balance tilts toward the top: because the benefit is a percentage of income, the biggest dollar gains go to owners of large, profitable pass-through businesses, while the permanent revenue loss is spread across all taxpayers through deficits or foregone public spending. A middle path — extending the deduction for a defined period or limiting it by income — was not part of this bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 118th Congress ended without a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Smucker introduced the bill on July 18, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
The bill attracted 194 cosponsors, including 192 of the House's 226 Republicans and two Democrats, Reps. Henry Cuellar and Josh Gottheimer.
The bill's only action beyond introduction was the committee referral; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote at any point.
The bill would have made permanent the qualified business income deduction, which under current law expires after December 31, 2025.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill was not carried over, so the deduction's scheduled expiration remains in effect unless a future Congress changes it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the scheduled 2025 expiration of the pass-through deduction stands and the Treasury keeps the revenue that permanence would have given up each year. Owners of profitable pass-through businesses did not get the tax break locked in permanently.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily one-sided: 192 of 226 House Republicans cosponsored the bill while only 2 of 216 House Democrats did.

industries.note: The bill would make their 20% income deduction permanent, and because the benefit is a percentage of income, the largest dollar gains go to owners of the most profitable enterprises. Their gain is paid for by permanent federal revenue loss that all taxpayers ultimately bear.

Genuinely small pass-through firms also claim the deduction and would gain certainty that it continues past 2025. Their dollar benefit is smaller than that of larger owners, since the deduction scales with income.

industries.industry: Federal Treasury and federal programs funded by income tax revenue
industries.note: The bill removes a scheduled revenue increase by making the deduction permanent, leaving less revenue for public priorities or more federal borrowing.
